To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
cholesterol and sphingolipopids are active partners in synaptic transmission".
cholesterol and sphingolipsids are active partners of neurotransmission, which are involved in the modulation of neurotransmitter binding, receptor conformation and signal transducing properties".
cholesterol and sphingol lipids are active partners of neurotransmission".
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular mechanisms of the interactions between neurotransmitter receptors and sphingolips/cholesterol.

the molecular mechanisms by which neurotransmitters and their cognate receptors interact with cholesterol and sphingomyelin, and how these lipids regulate the function of neurotransmitters and receptors in the nervous system.
the identification and characterization of the molecular mechanisms by which sphingolipid-cholesterol complexes regulate the conformational state of neurotransmitter receptors.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
sphingolipid-cholesterol regulation is a key factor in the molecular mechanism of synaptic transmission.

the biological functions (i.e., binding, activation, desensitization, internalization, recycling, etc.) of neurotransmitter receptors depend upon a dynamic equilibrium between cholesterol, sphingolipid, and neurotransmitter binding sites, which in turn may be regulated by the presence of other membrane lipids and/or proteins.
the biological functions and properties of neurotransmitters and of their receptors are highly regulated by sphingolipid-cholesterol interactions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
cholesterol and sphingoliphids are not only passive spectators, but active players in the regulation of neurotransmitter receptors".
the sphingolipid-cholesterol complex is a "chaperone" for neurotransmitters.
the biological function of neurotransmitter receptors is not only determined by the primary structure of the protein, but also by the nature of lipids surrounding the protein.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the molecular mechanisms involved are far more complex and sophisticated than a simple partitioning of receptors into lipid rafts.
sphingolipid-cholesterol interactions with neurotransmitter receptors should not be viewed as a simple "on/off" switch, but rather as a complex network of multiple and dynamic molecular interactions.
sphingolipid-cholesterol interactions with neurotransmitter receptors can be regarded as a new paradigm for the regulation of synaptic transmission.
